title: Creating Tables
narrative:
Swing-Tree exposes a user friendly API for defining tables in a declarative manner.
    You don't necessarily have to implement your own table model, because the Swing-Tree
    API allows you to supply simple collection based data as a data source for your table.

    Note that the **recommended** way of modelling a table is the `TableData` value,
    which describes an entire table (its cells, column names, column classes and layout)
    as a single immutable value that you hold in a property and bind to a table.
    See the `Table_Data_Spec` for what that looks like, and read on here for the older,
    pull based data sources, which are still supported and still handy for a quick table
    over data you already hold somewhere else.

features.id: A map can be used as a data source for tables.

extraInfo:
Note that you can actually pass a provider lambda for a map of header names to column lists to the table factory method and it will create a table model for you, which is based on the provided map provider. This will always result in a column major table.

Note that this data source is pull based: the table reads it whenever it feels like it, and it has no way of knowing when your map changed. Prefer a `TableData` value in a property (see the `Table_Data_Spec`) unless you really do have a map lying around which you would rather not copy.

features.id: We can pass an `Event` to the table model to trigger updates.

extraInfo:
Note that in this example we use a lambda based table model through the `withModel(Configurator)` method. This is a convenient way to create a table model without having to implement the TableModel interface yourself.

Observe how the `Event` has to be fired by hand after the data changed, and how the table can then only rebuild itself wholesale, because the event does not say what changed. A `TableData` value in a property (see the `Table_Data_Spec`) needs neither: it updates itself, and it knows exactly which rows moved.

features.id: A table can update itself reactively when bound to an `Observable`.

extraInfo:
Binding to an `Observable` is the most versatile and generic way of updating a table reactively.
            This observable may be derived from things like properties, property lists or a simple `Event`.
            You may declare them in you view model and expose observables derived from them to your view to then bind
            to your tables. Changes in your VM will then automatically update the table!

features.id: Configure which cells are editable or not as part of the table model declaration.

extraInfo:
The data model builder API allows you to define a lambda based table model
            where you can also specify if a cell is editable or not
            based on the row and column index.

            In the example below we define a table model where the cells are editable
            based on a flag and the condition `(r==1 || c==0)`.

features.id: Use `withCell(Configurator)` to configure both a renderer and editor for your table.

extraInfo:
The `withCell(Configurator)` method constitutes a useful API point
            which exposes you to a fluent API for configuring how a particular cell
            should be displayed.

            The `Configurator` lambda passed to the `withCell` method receives
            a delegate object of a particular cell in the table.
            You may update and return this cell with a view component
            used for either rendering, editing or both.

            So this may look like this:
            ```java
                .withCell( it -> it
                    .view( comp -> comp
                        .orGetUiIf(cell.isEditing(), {UI.textField().withBackground(Color.MAGENTA)})
                        .orGetUiIf(!cell.isEditing(), {UI.label("")})
                        .updateIf(JLabel.class, label -> {
                            label.text = "Day: " + cell.valueAsString().orElse("")
                            return label
                        })
                    )
                )
            ```
            Here you can see that the `Configurator` lambda receives a `cell` object
            which is a delegate object of a particular cell in the combo box.
            The view of this cell is updated with a text field or a label depending
            on whether the cell is currently being edited or not.

features.id: Fixed column names declared through `colNames(..)` also determine the column count.

extraInfo:
When you declare a fixed array of column names using the
            `colNames(String...)` method, you usually do not have to
            declare a `colCount(..)` lambda anymore, because the number
            of column names already implies the number of columns.

The column count is inferred from the two column names.

Asking the model for a name outside of the declared range yields an empty string rather than an error.

features.id: Fixed column classes declared through `colClasses(..)` imply the column count and default names.

extraInfo:
The `colClasses(Class...)` method defines the types of the
            individual columns, which a `JTable` uses to pick appropriate
            renderers and editors (a checkbox for booleans for example).

            Just like with `colNames(..)`, the number of declared classes
            implies the column count if you do not specify one.
            And if you do not declare any column names either, the simple
            names of the column classes serve as default column names.

features.id: Use `setsEntryAt(..)` to receive the edits a user makes through the table.

extraInfo:
The `getsEntryAt(..)` lambda feeds data into the table, and the
            `setsEntryAt(..)` lambda is its counterpart which channels user
            edits back out of the table and into your data structure.
            Note that for edits to reach the setter in a real application,
            the cells also have to be declared editable using `isEditableIf(..)`.

features.id: A table model without any configuration is empty, but does not blow up.

extraInfo:
All aspects of the lambda based table model are optional.

            no rows, no columns, `null` entries, no editability and
            silently ignored edits.

features.id: Firing the `updateOn` event notifies the table model listeners and refreshes the values.

extraInfo:
This is a regression guard for the lambda based table model update path.
            When the bound `updateOn` event fires, the model must notify its
            registered `TableModelListener`s (so a `JTable` repaints) and the
            values served afterwards must reflect the new state of the data.

features.id: Every aspect of a lambda based table model may only be declared once.

extraInfo:
The `BasicTableModel.Builder` fails fast when you accidentally
            declare the same model aspect twice, because the second declaration
            would silently override the first one, which is most likely a bug
            in the declaration. So instead of guessing which lambda you meant,
            it throws an `IllegalStateException` right away.

We try to define a second row count lambda...
...the builder complains immediately.
A null lambda on the other hand is reported as an invalid argument.

features.id: A property of a `Tuple` of `Tuple`s can be used as a data source for tables.

extraInfo:
The most convenient way to model the data of a table is a property
            holding a `Tuple` of `Tuple`s of cell values, a matrix of rows.
            Because a `Tuple` is immutable, such a table is thread safe by
            construction, and because the property is observable, the table
            updates itself whenever the property changes. So unlike for the
            collection based data sources, you do not need to bind an update
            `Event` through `updateTableOn(..)`.

We replace the entire tuple with a completely different one...
...the table follows, including the new column count.

features.id: The layout of a `Tuple` based table can be configured to be column major.

extraInfo:
Just like for the list based data sources, you may tell the table
            how to interpret the matrix you hand it, through one of the
            `UI.ListData` constants. In a column major layout the outer `Tuple`
            holds the columns of the table and each inner `Tuple` the cells of
            a column, which the table transposes for you.

features.id: A `Tuple` based table is read only if either its layout or its property is read only. [0]

extraInfo:
Editability of a tuple based table needs two things: an editable
            layout, and a property which can actually receive the edit. A read
            only `Val` cannot, which is why it always yields a read only table,
            even if you ask for an editable layout. Any edit which sneaks in
            through the model API anyway is silently ignored instead of
            corrupting the table.

A table built from this property, with the given layout:
The table is only editable if both the layout and the property allow it.
We push an edit through the model API regardless...
...it is only honored if the table is actually editable.
We check every combination of layout and property mutability.

features.id: A `Tuple` based table survives empty, ragged and out of bounds data.

extraInfo:
A table is queried by Swing at times you do not control, which is why
            a tuple based table never throws at its data source boundaries:
            an empty tuple is simply an empty table, a ragged matrix is as wide
            as its longest row (with the missing cells reading as `null`), and
            any out of bounds read is answered with `null`.

blocks.text: A property holding a ragged matrix, including an empty row.
A table built from this property:
The table is as wide as the longest row.
The cells the shorter rows do not have are reported as null.
Reads beyond the bounds of the table are answered with null instead of an exception.
We empty the property completely...
...the table is empty, and still does not blow up when read.

features.id: A `Tuple` based table tolerates a property which currently holds no tuple at all.

extraInfo:
A nullable property is a natural way to model table data which has not
            arrived yet (or which went away again). Binding such a property must
            yield an empty table rather than an exception, no matter whether the
            property is mutable or read only, and the table must fill up as soon
            as the data arrives.

blocks.text: A mutable and a read only nullable property, neither holding a tuple yet.
A table bound to each of them:
Both tables read as empty instead of being broken.
The data arrives in the mutable property...
...the table fills up.
The data goes away again...
...the table empties out, again without any drama.

features.id: A `Tuple` based table translates a change of its property into the most targeted table events possible. [0]

extraInfo:
A `Tuple` does not merely tell you that it changed, it also tells you
            *how* it changed. A tuple based table exploits this: instead of
            blindly rebuilding itself on every change, it translates a row
            insertion into a `fireTableRowsInserted`, a removal into a
            `fireTableRowsDeleted` and an in place change into a
            `fireTableRowsUpdated`, which is what keeps updates to large tables
            cheap. Only a change which cannot be expressed as a single row range,
            or one which changes the shape of the table, makes it fall back to a
            full rebuild (a structure change followed by a data change).

A listener recording the table model events in a readable form.

blocks.text: We apply the given change to the property...
...the table fired exactly the expected events...
...and it displays exactly the expected rows.
We cover every kind of change a tuple of rows may undergo.

features.id: A `Tuple` based table translates a change of its property into the most targeted table events possible. [10]

extraInfo:
A `Tuple` does not merely tell you that it changed, it also tells you
            *how* it changed. A tuple based table exploits this: instead of
            blindly rebuilding itself on every change, it translates a row
            insertion into a `fireTableRowsInserted`, a removal into a
            `fireTableRowsDeleted` and an in place change into a
            `fireTableRowsUpdated`, which is what keeps updates to large tables
            cheap. Only a change which cannot be expressed as a single row range,
            or one which changes the shape of the table, makes it fall back to a
            full rebuild (a structure change followed by a data change).

features.id: A property of a `TableData` can be used as a data source for tables.

extraInfo:
A `TableData` is the most complete description of the contents of
            a table: it carries the cells, the column names, the column classes and
            the layout of the data, all in a single immutable value. So if you hold
            such a value in a property, then that property alone describes your
            whole table, which is why you may bind it directly.
            Note that no `updateTableOn(..)` binding is needed here, because the
            table listens to the property itself.

The table displays everything the data describes.
The column names and classes reach the table as well.
We add a row to the data held by the property...
...the table shows the new row.

features.id: A `TableData` property based table is read only if either its layout or its property is read only. [0]

extraInfo:
Just like for a `Tuple` based table, two conditions have to be met before
            the user may edit the cells of a `TableData` based table: the layout
            of the snapshot has to be one of the `*_EDITABLE` constants, and the
            property has to be a mutable `Var` which can actually receive the edit.
            If either is missing, then the table is simply read only.

features.id: A `Var` exposed as a read only `Val` cannot be edited through the table.

extraInfo:
A view model routinely keeps its state in a `Var` but exposes only a read
            only `Val` of it to the outside (a `public Val<TableData> tableModel()`
            over a `private Var<TableData>`, say). If such a `Val` is bound through the
            read only `withModel(Val)` overload, then the table must be read only, no
            matter that the reference happens to point at a mutable `Var` at runtime:
            the overload the user picked is what expresses the intent, not the runtime
            type of the property. Anything else would let edits leak into state the
            view model never meant to expose.

blocks.text: A mutable `Var` holding an editable snapshot.

A table bound to it through the read only overload. The `(Val)` cast
                is what picks that overload here, just as a Java caller holding a
                `Val` reference (a view model exposing its `Var` as a `Val`, say)
                would pick it, rather than Groovy dispatching on the runtime `Var`.
The table reports its cells as read only, despite the mutable backing.
An edit is forced through the model API regardless...
...it is silently ignored: neither the table nor the backing property change.

features.id: The cells of an editable `TableData` based table are written back into the property.

extraInfo:
A `Var` holding an editable `TableData` is a two way binding: an edit
            made through the table model finds its way back into the property, and the
            property in turn is what the table reads. Note that the snapshot is a value,
            so the property receives a new snapshot rather than a mutated one.

blocks.text: A property holding an editable snapshot, and a table bound to it.
We remember the initial snapshot, so that we can tell it was not mutated.
The user edits a cell of the table...
...the edit is written back into the property.
The table displays the new value as well.
The snapshot the property held before the edit is untouched.

features.id: A change of the column names of a `TableData` property reaches the table.

extraInfo:
The columns of a table are not just its cells: a `TableData` also describes the name and class of every column. A `JTable` can only pick those up through a table structure change, so the model has to recognize a change of the columns as being structural.

Note how deliberate this is: below we rename a column and edit a row in one and the same change. The row edit alone would be synced through a targeted row update (the cells carry a diff which says so), and a row update would leave the table sitting on its old header. Recognizing the renamed column is what makes the model fall back to a full rebuild here.
